implementation_notes: C has no operator overloading, so a monoid is a struct of two function pointers - one producing the identity, one combining two values - and the fold is a generic loop that takes them plus an accumulator. Keeping the combine by pointer and the identity as a function (rather than a static value) is what lets the same fold run over arrays, linked lists or streams of any element type. This is also the right shape when the combine is expensive: the accumulate callback can carry the partial state in the accumulator pointer rather than in a fresh allocation.
idiom_name: struct of two function pointers (identity + combine) with a generic accumulator loop
pitfalls: The fold takes a const void* plus a stride, so a mistake in the stride silently aggregates the wrong bytes - there is no type checking to catch it.
An identity function that mallocs per call defeats the point when the fold is in a loop; return a shared static or a value in a caller-provided slot.
Aliasing the combine: writing to the second operand's memory to save an allocation turns an associative API into one whose result depends on evaluation order.
